questions.scenario: A Lambda function must process a batch of 10 SQS messages where message 4 fails. Without partial batch response configured, what happens to messages 1 to 3?
options: They are deleted because they succeeded
The entire batch returns to the queue and all 10 are reprocessed
Only message 4 returns to the queue
The batch is sent to the dead-letter queue immediately
questions.explain: Without ReportBatchItemFailures, Lambda deletes the batch only if the whole invocation succeeds. A single failure means none are deleted, so all 10 become visible again and successful messages are reprocessed — which is why consumers must be idempotent, or partial batch response should be enabled.

questions.scenario: An application must store items where the same logical record is updated frequently by multiple writers. Which DynamoDB pattern prevents lost updates?
options: Optimistic locking using a version attribute and a condition expression
Read the item, modify it, and write it back
BatchWriteItem
Scan then PutItem
questions.explain: Optimistic locking writes with a condition that the version attribute still matches what was read, so a competing update causes the write to fail and the caller retries with fresh data. Plain read-modify-write silently loses one update when two writers interleave, and batch or scan-based approaches do not address concurrency at all.

questions.scenario: An application must handle 1 million events per hour with ordering per user and the ability for three teams to consume independently. Which service fits BEST?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with user ID as the partition key
Amazon SQS standard queue
Amazon SQS FIFO queue
Amazon SNS
questions.explain: Kinesis preserves ordering within a shard selected by partition key, and multiple consumers read the same records independently at their own positions. SQS queues deliver each message to a single consumer, so three independent consumers would need three queues, and SNS provides no ordering guarantee.

questions.scenario: A developer must reduce the cold start time of a Java Lambda function with heavy initialisation. Which change helps MOST without provisioned concurrency?
options: Move heavy initialisation out of the critical path or use Lambda SnapStart where supported
Increase the timeout
Add more layers
Increase the batch size
questions.explain: Cold start cost is dominated by initialisation work, so deferring non-essential setup and trimming dependencies shortens it, while SnapStart takes a snapshot of the initialised environment and restores it for supported Java runtimes. Timeouts, layers and batch size do not affect initialisation time.

questions.scenario: Which TWO conditions cause DynamoDB to throttle requests?
options: A single partition receiving more traffic than its share of provisioned capacity
A global secondary index with insufficient provisioned write capacity
Items smaller than 1 KB
Using eventually consistent reads
Having fewer than 5 attributes per item
questions.explain: Capacity is distributed across partitions, so a hot partition throttles even when the table has spare capacity overall, and an under-provisioned GSI applies back-pressure that throttles base table writes. Small items, eventually consistent reads and attribute counts reduce or do not affect capacity consumption.

questions.scenario: An application must invoke a Lambda function when a CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM state. What is the correct configuration?
options: Configure the alarm action to publish to an SNS topic with the Lambda function subscribed, or use an EventBridge rule on the alarm state change
Poll CloudWatch every minute from the function
Attach the function to the alarm directly as a metric
Use an S3 event notification
questions.explain: Alarms publish state changes to SNS, and Lambda can subscribe to that topic, while EventBridge can also match alarm state change events directly. Polling wastes invocations and adds latency, functions cannot be attached to alarms as metrics, and S3 notifications relate to object operations.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct way to handle a Lambda function that must process items until a time budget is nearly exhausted?
options: Check the remaining execution time from the context object and stop cleanly before the timeout
Set the timeout to 15 minutes and ignore the budget
Catch the timeout exception
Use a fixed item count regardless of duration
questions.explain: The context object exposes remaining execution time, so a function can process until a safe threshold and then return cleanly with a continuation marker rather than being killed mid-work. Lambda does not raise a catchable timeout exception, and a fixed item count ignores variation in per-item cost.

questions.scenario: An application must deliver a message to a queue only after a downstream system confirms readiness, which may take hours. Which design is BEST?
options: Use Step Functions with waitForTaskToken so the workflow resumes when the downstream system calls back
Use an SQS delay queue
Poll the downstream system every minute from a Lambda function
Set a 12-hour visibility timeout
questions.explain: The callback pattern pauses the workflow until an external system supplies the task token, which suits waits measured in hours with no polling cost. SQS delays cap at 15 minutes, minute-by-minute polling wastes invocations for hours, and visibility timeout controls redelivery rather than waiting for an external signal.

questions.scenario: Which statement about API Gateway HTTP APIs versus REST APIs is correct?
options: HTTP APIs are lower cost and lower latency with a reduced feature set, lacking features such as request validation and usage plans
HTTP APIs support every REST API feature
REST APIs are always cheaper
HTTP APIs cannot integrate with Lambda
questions.explain: HTTP APIs are cheaper and faster but omit several REST API capabilities including request validation, usage plans, API keys and caching, so the choice depends on which of those features are required. They integrate with Lambda and HTTP backends normally.

questions.scenario: A developer must ensure a DynamoDB write only proceeds if an item's status is currently PENDING. What should be used?
options: A condition expression checking the status attribute
A filter expression
A scan for the status first, then a write
A global secondary index on status
questions.explain: A condition expression evaluates atomically at write time, so the write succeeds only if the status is still PENDING and otherwise fails cleanly. Reading first and writing afterwards leaves a race window, filter expressions apply to reads, and an index changes query patterns rather than enforcing write conditions.

questions.scenario: An application must process a Kinesis stream where one shard consistently lags. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A hot partition key sending disproportionate traffic to that shard
Insufficient stream retention
Too many consumers
The region is misconfigured
questions.explain: Records are assigned to shards by hashing the partition key, so a dominant key value concentrates traffic on one shard and its consumer falls behind while others keep up. A higher-cardinality or composite key spreads the load. Retention, consumer count and region do not cause per-shard skew.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct approach for a Lambda function that must write to a resource in a peered VPC?
options: Attach the function to subnets in the local VPC with routes to the peered VPC and appropriate security group rules
Attach the function to the peered VPC directly
Use a NAT gateway in the peered VPC
Make the resource public
questions.explain: A function attaches to subnets in one VPC, and reaching a peered VPC requires route table entries and security group rules permitting the traffic. It cannot be attached to a VPC it does not have subnets in, a NAT gateway provides outbound internet rather than peering, and exposing the resource publicly is a security regression.

questions.scenario: Which statement about SQS message attributes is correct?
options: They carry structured metadata separate from the body and can be used by SNS subscription filter policies
They count toward a separate size limit from the body
They are encrypted separately
They are required for FIFO queues
questions.explain: Message attributes provide structured metadata alongside the body, and SNS filter policies evaluate them to decide delivery. They count toward the same 256 KB total size limit as the body, share the same encryption, and are optional for both queue types.

questions.scenario: An application must guarantee that a workflow step is not executed twice even if the workflow is retried. What is required?
options: Make the step idempotent, for example with a conditional write keyed on the execution or request identifier
Rely on Step Functions to prevent duplicates
Disable retries
Use a Wait state
questions.explain: Retries can re-execute a step whose side effect already occurred, so the step itself must be idempotent — typically enforced with a conditional write keyed on a unique identifier. Step Functions does not deduplicate side effects, disabling retries sacrifices resilience, and waiting changes timing rather than semantics.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST supports an API that must return partial results quickly while slower data loads?
options: Return the fast data immediately and let the client fetch the slower portion separately, or use response streaming
Wait for all data before responding
Increase the API Gateway timeout
Cache the slow data indefinitely
questions.explain: Splitting the response so fast data returns immediately keeps perceived latency low, and response streaming can deliver data progressively where supported. Waiting for everything makes the slowest component dictate the response time, the 29-second gateway limit cannot be raised, and caching indefinitely serves stale data.

questions.scenario: A developer must choose between storing a computed value and recomputing it on each read. The value is expensive to compute and read 1,000 times per write. What is BEST?
options: Store the computed value and update it on write
Recompute on every read
Recompute on a schedule regardless of writes
Store the value but never update it
questions.explain: With a thousand reads per write, computing once at write time and storing the result amortises the cost across all those reads. Recomputing per read pays the expensive operation a thousand times, scheduled recomputation serves stale data between runs, and never updating makes it permanently wrong.

questions.scenario: Which is true about Lambda function URLs?
options: They provide a dedicated HTTPS endpoint for a function with optional IAM authentication, without API Gateway
They require API Gateway
They support usage plans and API keys
They provide request validation
questions.explain: Function URLs give a function its own HTTPS endpoint with either no authentication or IAM authentication, useful for simple webhooks without an API layer. They do not provide API Gateway features such as usage plans, API keys, request validation or caching.

questions.scenario: An application must ensure that an S3 object is not processed until a related database record exists. What is the MOST reliable design?
options: Write the database record first, then upload the object, and trigger processing from the upload
Upload the object first and retry processing until the record appears
Process immediately and ignore missing records
Poll the database every second
questions.explain: Ordering the writes so the dependency exists before the triggering event removes the race entirely. Uploading first and retrying wastes invocations and may never succeed if the record write failed, ignoring missing records corrupts state, and per-second polling is expensive and still racy.

questions.scenario: Which DynamoDB feature allows restoring a table to any second within the last 35 days?
options: Point-in-time recovery
On-demand backup
DynamoDB Streams
Global tables
questions.explain: Point-in-time recovery provides continuous backups allowing restoration to any second in the preceding 35 days, which protects against accidental writes and deletes. On-demand backups are discrete snapshots, Streams retain changes for 24 hours as a change log, and global tables replicate data rather than provide historical restore.

questions.scenario: An application must fan out an event to consumers in three different AWS accounts. Which service supports this MOST directly?
options: EventBridge with cross-account event buses or targets
SQS with cross-account polling
Lambda with cross-account invocation only
S3 event notifications
questions.explain: EventBridge supports cross-account delivery by granting other accounts permission on a bus or by targeting buses in other accounts, so each consumer manages its own rules. SQS and Lambda cross-account access is possible but requires per-consumer wiring, and S3 notifications target a limited set of same-account services.

questions.scenario: Which approach reduces the risk of a Lambda function exhausting a downstream connection pool?
options: Use RDS Proxy or a shared connection pool, and cap function concurrency
Increase the function timeout
Open a new connection per invocation
Disable connection reuse
questions.explain: Each concurrent execution environment holds its own connection, so high concurrency exhausts database connections. RDS Proxy pools and shares connections across invocations, and capping concurrency bounds demand. Longer timeouts hold connections longer, and opening new connections per invocation or disabling reuse makes the problem worse.

questions.scenario: Which is required for a Lambda function to publish to an SNS topic encrypted with a customer managed KMS key?
options: sns:Publish plus kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt on the key
sns:Publish only
kms:CreateKey
No additional permissions
questions.explain: Publishing to an encrypted topic requires the publisher to generate a data key and encrypt the payload, so the role needs kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt on the key in addition to sns:Publish. Missing the KMS permissions produces AccessDenied even though the SNS permission is correct.

questions.scenario: An application must ensure a user can only invoke an API method if they belong to a specific Cognito group. What is the cleanest implementation?
options: Check the cognito:groups claim in a Lambda authorizer or in the application, returning a policy or rejecting the request
Rely on the user pool to enforce it automatically
Use an API key per group
Trust a client-supplied group header
questions.explain: Group membership appears in the token's cognito:groups claim, and an authorizer or the application evaluates it to allow or deny. User pools authenticate rather than enforce per-method authorisation, API keys are for metering, and any client-supplied header is trivially forged.

questions.scenario: Which practice ensures that an application's IAM permissions match what it actually uses?
options: Review IAM Access Advisor last-accessed data and generate policies from CloudTrail activity
Grant broad permissions and monitor
Copy policies from another service
Use wildcards to avoid future errors
questions.explain: Last-accessed data reveals permissions that are never exercised and can be removed, and generating policies from observed CloudTrail activity produces least-privilege policies grounded in real usage. Broad permissions, copied policies and wildcards all grant more than necessary.

questions.scenario: Which statement about presigned URLs for S3 uploads is correct?
options: The URL can restrict the key, method, expiry and required headers such as content type or encryption
The URL allows any operation on the bucket
The URL never expires
The URL requires the bucket to be public
questions.explain: A presigned URL encodes the specific operation, object key, expiry and any headers included in the signature, and the client's request must match or S3 rejects it. It grants only that operation, always carries an expiry, and works with private buckets — which is the point.

questions.scenario: Which TWO reduce the risk of privilege escalation through IAM?
options: Restrict iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs
Apply permission boundaries to roles that can create other roles
Grant iam:* to developers for convenience
Allow any principal to assume any role
Disable CloudTrail for IAM events
questions.explain: Unrestricted iam:PassRole lets a principal attach a highly privileged role to a resource they control, and permission boundaries cap whatever a role-creating principal can produce. Blanket IAM permissions and unrestricted role assumption enable exactly the escalation being prevented, and disabling CloudTrail removes the ability to detect it.

questions.scenario: An application must encrypt a field in DynamoDB such that only a specific service can read it, even though several services can read the table. What approach works?
options: Client-side encrypt the field with a KMS key whose policy grants decrypt only to that service
Rely on DynamoDB encryption at rest
Store the field in a separate table with the same permissions
Base64-encode the field
questions.explain: Encryption at rest protects storage but every reader of the table sees plaintext, so field-level client-side encryption with a restricted KMS key is what limits readability to one service. A separate table with identical permissions changes nothing, and base64 is reversible encoding rather than encryption.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct configuration to require MFA for deleting objects in a versioned S3 bucket?
options: Enable MFA Delete on the bucket, configured by the bucket owner using root credentials
Add an IAM policy requiring MFA for GetObject
Enable versioning only
Enable Block Public Access
questions.explain: MFA Delete requires a multi-factor code to permanently delete object versions or change the versioning state, and it can only be enabled by the bucket owner using root credentials. Requiring MFA for reads does not protect deletions, and versioning alone permits deletion while Block Public Access governs public exposure.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST protects an application from a stolen JWT being used indefinitely?
options: Short access token lifetimes with refresh tokens, plus the ability to revoke sessions
Long-lived access tokens for convenience
Storing tokens in localStorage
Validating only the signature
questions.explain: Short-lived access tokens limit how long a stolen token remains usable, and refresh tokens allow revocation to end a session. Long-lived tokens extend the damage window, localStorage increases exposure to cross-site scripting, and validating only the signature ignores expiry entirely.

questions.scenario: Which statement about AWS Certificate Manager certificates is correct?
options: Public certificates are free and auto-renew when used with supported AWS services, but must be in us-east-1 for CloudFront
Certificates cost per request
Certificates never renew
Certificates can be exported for use anywhere
questions.explain: ACM public certificates are free and renew automatically when attached to supported services, and CloudFront specifically requires the certificate in us-east-1. There is no per-request charge, and public ACM certificates cannot be exported — that requires AWS Private CA.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct way to grant a partner temporary access to upload to a specific S3 prefix without AWS credentials?
options: Generate presigned URLs server-side for the specific keys, with short expiry
Create an IAM user and share the keys
Make the prefix publicly writable
Share the bucket policy
questions.explain: Presigned URLs grant a specific operation on a specific key for a limited time without the partner ever holding AWS credentials. IAM user keys are long-lived and hard to revoke cleanly, a publicly writable prefix accepts uploads from anyone, and sharing a policy document grants nothing.

questions.scenario: Which practice reduces the risk that logs sent to a third-party service leak sensitive data?
options: Redact or omit sensitive fields at the source before shipping logs anywhere
Encrypt logs in transit only
Ship all logs and filter at the destination
Rely on the vendor's access controls
questions.explain: Removing sensitive data before it leaves the application means it never reaches the third party at all, which is the only control fully within your governance. Transport encryption protects the wire but the vendor still receives plaintext, and filtering at the destination or trusting vendor controls means the data has already left your boundary.

questions.scenario: Which statement about service control policies is correct?
options: They set the maximum available permissions for accounts in an organisation and never grant permissions themselves
They grant permissions directly to principals
They apply only to the management account
They replace IAM policies
questions.explain: An SCP is a permission ceiling: an action must be allowed by both the SCP and an IAM policy to succeed, and the SCP alone grants nothing. SCPs apply to member accounts rather than the management account and complement rather than replace IAM policies.

questions.scenario: An application must verify that a request came from Amazon API Gateway and not directly to the backend. What is the correct approach?
options: Restrict the backend so only API Gateway can invoke it, for example with a Lambda resource policy or a VPC link and security groups
Check a custom header set by the client
Compare the source IP to a public list
Trust the user agent
questions.explain: Enforcing the restriction in IAM or the network means the backend simply cannot be reached by anything except API Gateway. Client-supplied headers and user agents are trivially forged, and API Gateway source addresses are dynamic so IP allowlists are unreliable.

questions.scenario: Which is true about rotating a secret used by many services simultaneously?
options: An alternating users or dual-credential strategy avoids downtime because the old credential stays valid during the transition
All services must restart at the same moment
Rotation always causes downtime
Only one service can use a secret
questions.explain: Keeping two valid credentials and switching between them means services still holding the previous value continue working while they pick up the new one, so rotation is transparent. Coordinated simultaneous restarts are fragile, and a secret can serve many consumers.

questions.scenario: Which control prevents an application from accidentally sending production data to a development account?
options: Restrict cross-account permissions and use SCPs plus resource policies limiting which accounts can be targeted
Rely on naming conventions
Use the same credentials everywhere
Disable CloudTrail
questions.explain: Explicit cross-account restrictions make sending data to an unintended account impossible rather than merely discouraged. Naming conventions rely on human care, shared credentials remove the account boundary entirely, and disabling CloudTrail removes the ability to detect mistakes.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct interpretation of an S3 access log entry showing a 403 for an authenticated request?
options: The request was authenticated but not authorised — a policy, ACL, Block Public Access setting or missing KMS permission denied it
The credentials were invalid
The object does not exist
The request timed out
questions.explain: A 403 means the identity was established but the action was denied, so the cause lies in an explicit deny, a missing allow, Block Public Access, or missing kms:Decrypt for an encrypted object. Invalid credentials produce a different error, a missing object gives 404, and timeouts do not return 403.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST secures an application that must accept file uploads from untrusted users?
options: Upload to a quarantine location, validate content type and scan, then move to the processing location
Process uploads immediately in the main pipeline
Trust the client-supplied filename and content type
Store uploads in a public bucket
questions.explain: Isolating uploads until they are validated and scanned prevents malicious content reaching processing systems or other users. Immediate processing exposes the pipeline, client-supplied metadata is unreliable, and a public bucket allows anyone to retrieve unvalidated content.

questions.scenario: Which CloudFormation feature allows a template to adapt resource properties based on the deployment region?
options: Mappings keyed on region, referenced with Fn::FindInMap
Outputs
Metadata
DependsOn
questions.explain: Mappings provide static lookup tables commonly keyed on region — for example AMI IDs — retrieved with Fn::FindInMap. Outputs export values, Metadata carries arbitrary information, and DependsOn orders resource creation.

questions.scenario: A team must deploy a change that adds a required field to an API request. What deployment approach avoids breaking existing clients?
options: Make the field optional first, migrate clients, then make it required in a later release
Make it required immediately
Deploy a new API and delete the old one
Reject requests without the field from day one
questions.explain: Introducing the field as optional keeps existing clients working while they migrate, and only once all traffic includes it does making it required become safe. Requiring it immediately, or rejecting requests without it, breaks every client that has not yet updated, and deleting the old API removes their only working endpoint.

questions.scenario: Which is true about CodeBuild environment variables of type PARAMETER_STORE or SECRETS_MANAGER?
options: The value is resolved at build time and the service role needs permission to read it
The value is stored in plaintext in the buildspec
They cannot be used in a pipeline
They are only available in the install phase
questions.explain: These variable types reference a parameter or secret by name and resolve at build time, so no plaintext secret appears in the buildspec or project configuration, provided the service role can read it. They are available throughout the build and work within pipelines.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST allows a team to test infrastructure changes without affecting shared environments?
options: Deploy a personal ephemeral stack from the same template with a unique name prefix, then delete it
Modify the shared development stack
Test directly in production
Skip testing infrastructure changes
questions.explain: An ephemeral personal stack exercises the real template in isolation and disappears afterwards, so no shared environment is disturbed and cost is bounded. Modifying shared development blocks colleagues, production testing risks outages, and skipping testing means the first real deployment is the experiment.

questions.scenario: Which statement about Lambda aliases and traffic shifting is correct?
options: An alias can route a weighted percentage of traffic between two versions, which is how canary deployments work
Aliases can only point to one version
Aliases shift traffic instantly only
Aliases apply to layers
questions.explain: An alias supports weighted routing between two versions, which CodeDeploy adjusts progressively during canary and linear deployments. That weighting is precisely what enables gradual rollout and instant rollback, and aliases apply to function versions rather than layers.

questions.scenario: Which practice reduces the chance that a deployment succeeds technically but breaks user-facing behaviour?
options: Run automated smoke tests against the deployed environment as a pipeline stage before promotion
Rely on unit tests only
Check the CloudFormation status only
Deploy and wait for user reports
questions.explain: Smoke tests exercise real endpoints after deployment and fail the pipeline before promotion if behaviour is wrong. Unit tests do not validate a deployed system, a successful stack status only means resources were created, and waiting for user reports means users find the defect first.

questions.scenario: Which TWO help ensure a pipeline is reproducible?
options: Pin build tool and runtime versions explicitly
Commit lockfiles for dependencies
Use the latest tag for base images
Install dependencies from unpinned sources
Rely on the developer's local environment
questions.explain: Pinning tool and runtime versions and committing lockfiles means the same inputs produce the same output regardless of when the build runs. Mutable base image tags, unpinned dependency sources and local environment assumptions all introduce variation that makes builds non-reproducible.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct way to deploy a change that requires both an infrastructure update and a code change atomically?
options: Define both in the same CloudFormation or SAM template so the stack update applies them together with rollback on failure
Deploy them separately and hope the ordering works
Deploy code first, then infrastructure manually
Deploy infrastructure by hand in the console
questions.explain: Managing both in one stack means CloudFormation applies them as a single unit and rolls back together if anything fails, avoiding a mismatched intermediate state. Separate or manual deployments create windows where code and infrastructure disagree, and console changes bypass version control entirely.

questions.scenario: Which statement about ECS service auto scaling is correct?
options: It adjusts the desired task count based on CloudWatch metrics such as CPU utilisation or request count per target
It resizes individual tasks
It only works with the EC2 launch type
It requires manual intervention
questions.explain: Service auto scaling changes how many tasks run in response to target tracking or step scaling policies on CloudWatch metrics. Task CPU and memory are fixed by the task definition rather than resized dynamically, and it works with both Fargate and EC2 launch types automatically.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST manages secrets needed during a CodeBuild build, such as a private registry token?
options: Reference Secrets Manager or Parameter Store from the project's environment variables so the value never appears in the buildspec
Commit the token to the repository
Echo the token in the build log for verification
Pass it as a plaintext environment variable in the console
questions.explain: Referencing a secret by name resolves it at build time with the service role's permission, keeping the plaintext out of source control, project configuration and logs. Committing tokens, printing them to logs, or storing them as plaintext variables all create durable copies that are hard to revoke.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST likely reason a CloudFormation stack update takes far longer than expected?
options: A resource requiring replacement is being recreated, such as a database or an instance
The template has too many comments
Too many parameters are defined
The stack name is long
questions.explain: Replacement means creating a new resource and deleting the old one, which for databases or instances can take a very long time — and a change set would have flagged it in advance. Comments, parameter counts and naming have no effect on deployment duration.

questions.scenario: Which practice supports safely deploying to multiple regions?
options: Deploy to one region first, verify with automated checks, then progress to remaining regions
Deploy everywhere simultaneously
Deploy manually in each region
Deploy only to one region and route all traffic there
questions.explain: Progressive regional rollout limits the blast radius so a defect affects one region while automated checks decide whether to continue. Simultaneous deployment exposes every region at once, manual deployment causes drift, and single-region deployment abandons the multi-region requirement.

questions.scenario: Which statement about the SAM CLI's sam local start-api is correct?
options: It emulates API Gateway locally using Docker so functions can be invoked over HTTP during development
It deploys the API to AWS
It requires an internet connection to AWS
It replaces integration testing
questions.explain: sam local start-api runs functions in Docker containers behind a local HTTP endpoint that mimics API Gateway, giving fast feedback without deploying. It does not deploy anything, works offline once images are cached, and does not substitute for testing against real AWS services.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct approach when a deployment must be rolled back but the new version already wrote incompatible data?
options: Prevent the situation by designing forward-compatible data changes; otherwise a data migration or restore is required alongside the code rollback
Roll back the code and ignore the data
Delete the affected data
Roll forward only, never back
questions.explain: Once incompatible data exists, a code rollback alone leaves the old version unable to read it, so the durable answer is designing changes the previous version can tolerate. When that has not been done, the data must be migrated or restored as part of the rollback. Ignoring or deleting data causes correctness problems or loss.

questions.scenario: Which pipeline practice MOST reduces the time between a defect being introduced and detected?
options: Run fast automated tests on every commit, with slower suites later in the pipeline
Test weekly
Test only before releases
Rely on manual testing
questions.explain: Running fast tests on every commit surfaces defects within minutes while the change is fresh, and deferring slower suites keeps that feedback quick without losing coverage. Weekly or release-only testing lets defects accumulate, and manual testing is slow and inconsistent.

questions.scenario: An application's error rate rises only when a specific downstream service is deployed. What does this suggest?
options: A compatibility problem between the two services, such as a contract change without backward compatibility
A CloudWatch problem
A DNS issue
A billing issue
questions.explain: Errors correlating precisely with a dependency's deployments points to a contract or behaviour change the caller cannot handle, which is the case backward-compatible API evolution exists to prevent. Monitoring, DNS and billing problems would not align with another team's release schedule.

questions.scenario: Which is the BEST way to detect a slow memory leak in a Lambda function?
options: Track Max Memory Used from REPORT lines over many invocations and look for a rising trend within warm environments
Check a single invocation
Increase memory and stop monitoring
Rely on the Errors metric
questions.explain: Because execution environments persist, memory used should be compared across many invocations in the same environment, where a leak shows as a steadily climbing baseline. One invocation reveals nothing about the trend, raising memory only delays the failure, and errors appear only once memory is exhausted.

questions.scenario: Which observation indicates that adding read replicas would NOT solve a database performance problem?
options: The workload is write-heavy and writes are the bottleneck
Read latency is high
Read volume exceeds the primary's capacity
Reports run long read queries
questions.explain: Read replicas scale read capacity only, so a write-bound workload gains nothing and may even suffer from added replication overhead. Sharding, write batching or a different data model addresses write bottlenecks. The other scenarios are all read-bound and benefit from replicas.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST effective way to reduce the impact of a noisy neighbour consuming shared Lambda concurrency?
options: Set reserved concurrency on the noisy function to cap its share of the account pool
Increase the account concurrency limit only
Reduce the memory of other functions
Disable the noisy function
questions.explain: Reserved concurrency caps how much of the shared pool one function may consume, guaranteeing headroom for everything else. Raising the account limit is a blunt and costlier response that leaves the imbalance in place, memory does not affect concurrency, and disabling the function removes needed capability.

questions.scenario: An application must determine whether a latency spike affected all users or only some. What is the MOST direct analysis?
options: Break latency down by dimension such as region, client version or endpoint, and compare percentiles across segments
Look at the overall average only
Count total requests
Check the deployment history only
questions.explain: Segmenting the metric reveals whether degradation is universal or confined to a subset, which immediately narrows the cause. Overall averages hide segment differences, request counts measure volume, and deployment history is useful context but does not by itself show who was affected.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct interpretation of a CloudWatch metric with the Sum statistic for Lambda Errors?
options: It is the total count of failed invocations in the period, which should be compared against Invocations to derive a rate
It is the average error rate
It is the maximum errors per second
It is the number of functions
questions.explain: Errors with the Sum statistic gives an absolute count, which only becomes meaningful when divided by Invocations to produce a rate — a hundred errors matters very differently at a thousand versus a million invocations. Metric math can compute that ratio for alarming.

questions.scenario: Which practice MOST improves mean time to recovery during an incident?
options: Automated rollback plus runbooks and dashboards that quickly identify the failing component
Investigating the root cause fully before acting
Waiting for the next deployment window
Adding more metrics during the incident
questions.explain: Restoring service quickly through automated rollback, guided by runbooks and dashboards that localise the failure, minimises user impact — with root cause analysis following afterwards. Full investigation before acting extends the outage, waiting for a window prolongs it further, and instrumenting during an incident is too late.

questions.scenario: An application shows high latency only for the first request to each new execution environment, and traffic is steady but spread across many concurrent executions. What explains this?
options: Lambda scales out by creating new environments, and each new one pays initialisation cost
The function is throttled
The database is slow
The region is misconfigured
questions.explain: Steady traffic spread across high concurrency means Lambda continually creates new execution environments as it scales, and each pays initialisation cost on its first request. Provisioned concurrency or lighter initialisation reduces it. Throttling, database latency and region choice would not correlate with first-request-per-environment.

questions.scenario: Which is the BEST metric to alarm on for a queue-based asynchronous system?
options: Age of the oldest message, since it directly reflects processing delay
Total messages sent
Queue name length
Number of consumers
questions.explain: Oldest message age measures how long work has waited, which maps directly to the user-visible delay and rises whenever consumers cannot keep up. Messages sent measures inbound volume without indicating whether it is being processed, and queue naming and consumer counts are configuration rather than symptoms.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST identifies whether a performance regression came from a code change or an infrastructure change?
options: Correlate the regression's start time with both deployment and infrastructure change events recorded in CloudTrail and pipeline history
Check application logs only
Restart all services
Increase capacity
questions.explain: Aligning the regression's onset with recorded deployments and infrastructure changes usually identifies the trigger immediately. Logs alone may show symptoms without the cause, restarting can mask the problem temporarily, and adding capacity treats the symptom without identifying the change responsible.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST effective way to reduce the cost of a CloudWatch dashboard refreshed continuously by many users?
options: Reduce the number of metrics and widgets and lengthen the refresh interval, since dashboard API calls are billed
Add more widgets
Increase metric resolution
Duplicate the dashboard per user
questions.explain: Dashboard metric retrieval generates billable API calls that multiply with widget count, refresh frequency and concurrent viewers. Fewer widgets and a longer refresh interval reduce all three factors. More widgets, higher resolution and per-user duplicates all increase cost.

questions.scenario: Which practice BEST supports diagnosing an issue that occurred three days ago?
options: Retain logs, metrics and traces long enough to cover the investigation window, with retention set deliberately per data type
Set all retention to one day to save cost
Rely on memory of the incident
Disable tracing
questions.explain: Investigating a past incident requires the evidence to still exist, so retention must be set deliberately — long enough to be useful, short enough to control cost, and potentially different for logs, metrics and traces. One-day retention erases the evidence, recollection is unreliable, and disabling tracing removes it entirely.
